READING

**Laying out the arithmetic for TREVANNOCK**

The three Vantwyn seasons generate gross income of 400 × £168 = £67,200 per season.

Against that, three costs run each season:

| Item | Calculation | Per season |
|---|---|---|
| Borage forgone | 400 × £71 | £28,400 |
| Spray replacement | 9 % × 400 × £210 | £7,560 |
| Haulage and labour | given | £6,900 |
| **Total cost** | | **£42,860** |

Net per season: £67,200 − £42,860 = **£24,340**
Over three seasons: **£73,020**
Terminal kit value (post-permit): **£20,000**
Total value retained under TREVANNOCK: **£93,020**

**Comparing against ORMSCLEUCH**

Under ORMSCLEUCH the kit goes to Ravensgate now for £96,000. The 400 colonies stay on heather and borage and incur no spray losses and no haulage.

The kit differential is £96,000 − £20,000 = **£76,000 in favour of ORMSCLEUCH**. The three-season operating advantage of TREVANNOCK is **£73,020**. On straight nominal figures ORMSCLEUCH is already ahead by roughly £3,000.

That is before time value. The £96,000 is received today. The £20,000 is received at the far end of 2029, roughly 3½ years away. At a modest 5 % discount the terminal kit is worth about £16,850 in present terms, so the discounted kit gap rises to £79,150. The Vantwyn net flows are also future and must be discounted: at 5 %, the three-year stream of £24,340 sums to approximately £64,700 in present value. On a discounted basis ORMSCLEUCH leads by roughly **£14,000–£15,000**.

**Testing the spray-mortality assumption**

The 9 % figure is not an industry average or a projection—it is the recorded outcome for Whinnerdale Bees on the identical programme that Vantwyn will use. Vantwyn have stated that programme will not vary. That makes the 36 colony losses per season a near-certainty rather than a probability. If the actual rate is worse—12–15 % is plausible given that Whinnerdale's experience is already on record—the replacement bill rises to £10,000–£13,000 per season and the annual net from Vantwyn drops to £11,000–£17,000, making TREVANNOCK deeply loss-making against ORMSCLEUCH.

**The strategic case for TREVANNOCK**

Coldharbour and Nyefield are asking your rate for 2028. That is a genuine option value: if their contracts are viable they could extend the life of the migratory operation beyond Vantwyn's three seasons and justify keeping the lorry in the low-emission zone while it retains its permit. But that option has several weaknesses: (a) the migratory side was idle through all of 2025 and produced no contracts, having previously lost three in a row; (b) the permit expires 2030-01-01 regardless, so any extension is short; (c) being committed to Vantwyn through 2029 means the same spray-mortality risk runs through the seasons when Coldharbour and Nyefield would most likely start; and (d) keeping the operation going for speculative 2028 inquiries while the kit depreciates requires actual confirmed contracts to materialise within a year or two of the permit ceiling. That is a fragile chain.

**The simplicity argument**

ORMSCLEUCH converts a two-strand business—which has been running one strand at idle for a year—back into a single, well-understood honey operation. The £96,000 realised now can be redeployed into that operation (more colonies, better processing, marketing) where the return per colony was £223 last season. Every pound deployed on the home sites carries no spray risk and no haulage charge.

**The sunk-cost caveat**

The £187,000 spent in 2024 on pallets, the Hiab and the queen rearing shed is gone regardless of which course is taken. It should not tip the scales toward TREVANNOCK to avoid acknowledging it. The queen rearing shed is not mentioned in the Ravensgate offer, so its value is separate from this decision.

**Summary position**

| Criterion | TREVANNOCK | ORMSCLEUCH |
|---|---|---|
| Nominal 3-year value | £93,020 | £96,000 |
| PV of same | ~£81,550 | £96,000 |
| Spray-mortality risk | Material and documented | None |
| Haulage exposure | £20,700 over 3 seasons | Nil |
| Operational complexity | Two operations | One |
| Kit value after 2030 | ~£20,000 (farm vehicle) | Offer captured at £96,000 |
| Market optionality | Possible 2028 vale contracts | Foregone |

ORMSCLEUCH is better financially on both nominal and discounted measures. The risk-adjusted gap is wider still, because the spray losses are drawn from a real prior outcome rather than an assumed percentage. The strategic upside of remaining in the vale pollination market is real but rests on a run of three consecutive non-renewals and a migratory side that has produced no revenue for the entire 2025 season.

---

READING
  The discounted-value comparison comes out roughly £14,000–£15,000 in favour of ORMSCLEUCH before any risk adjustment; the Vantwyn spray mortality is documented rather than theoretical (same programme, same rate, a named predecessor); the nominal case for TREVANNOCK (£73,020 net operating gain vs £76,000 kit-value haircut) does not cover the gap even without discounting; and the strategic option value of the two vale growers asking for 2028 is too slender and contingent to close a deficit that only widens when time-value and known spray risk are applied.

CALL
  ORMSCLEUCH

GROUNDS
  Selling the kit captures a £76,000 nominal kit premium that three seasons of Vantwyn net income (£73,020) cannot match even before discounting or the documented spray-mortality risk from an identical programme is applied.
